title: Project: Documented School Initiative
subtitle: Learn to compare information and use evidence to support your ideas.
objectives: Identify reliable sources of information for school projects.
Compare different pieces of information to find the strongest evidence.
Present a school initiative proposal supported by concrete evidence.

scenes.title: What's Your Idea?
scenes.display: Got a great idea for school?
scenes.narration: Imagine an amazing school idea, like a new recycling program. How would you convince others it's good? You need more than just enthusiasm to make it happen.
scenes.visualAction: Student character excitedly drawing a lightbulb idea, then looking thoughtful.

scenes.title: Evidence Matters
scenes.narration: To make your idea happen, strong evidence is crucial. Evidence proves your point, showing why your idea is needed. Without it, even great ideas can be overlooked.
scenes.visualAction: Character points to a chart showing 'Idea' leading to 'Evidence' leading to 'Success'.

scenes.title: Finding Good Sources
scenes.narration: Find evidence from reliable sources like school records, surveys, or expert interviews. For example, consider gathering evidence for a new school book-swap program.
scenes.visualAction: Character scrolls through digital documents and a survey form, highlighting key facts.

scenes.title: Comparing Facts
scenes.narration: Compare information from different sources. Identify the most relevant and convincing facts. Strong evidence is specific, verifiable, and directly supports your claim, building a solid argument.
scenes.visualAction: Two different 'fact' bubbles appear side-by-side, then one glows brighter, indicating stronger evidence.

scenes.title: Making It Better
scenes.narration: Your first draft might need refining. Add specific evidence or clarify points. This review process strengthens your proposal, making your initiative much more persuasive.
scenes.visualAction: Character reviews a document, crosses out a weak sentence, and writes a stronger, evidence-backed one.

scenes.title: Your Turn to Plan
scenes.narration: Now, think of a school initiative. Gather evidence, compare findings, and draft a proposal. Clearly state your sources. This practice helps you present well-supported ideas.
scenes.visualAction: Character gestures towards a blank document, inviting the learner to start writing.

scenes.title: Share Your Vision
scenes.narration: You've learned to gather, compare, and use evidence. This skill is valuable for school projects and anything you want to achieve. Share your initiatives with confidence!
scenes.visualAction: Character stands proudly next to a completed project board, smiling.

reading.title: What is Evidence?
reading.text: Evidence is information that supports a claim or idea. It can be facts, statistics, examples, or expert opinions. Strong evidence is specific, relevant, and comes from a reliable source. It helps convince others that your idea is valid and well-thought-out.

reading.title: Using Evidence for a Book Swap
reading.text: For a school book-swap, evidence could be a survey showing students want more reading options, data on unused books at home, or a quote from a librarian about the benefits of book sharing. This proves the need and value of the initiative.

reading.title: Comparing Sources
reading.text: When comparing sources, ask: Is it current? Is the author an expert? Is it biased? Official school reports or academic studies are often more reliable than a personal blog post. Choose the most credible and relevant information.

materials.title: School Policy on Student Initiatives (Invented Teaching Example)
materials.text: Policy 3.1.2: The school prioritizes student-led initiatives that enhance student well-being and academic engagement. A recent internal report (School Board, 2023) noted that student participation in extracurricular reading programs has declined by 10% over the last two years. Proposals for new initiatives must include at least two distinct pieces of evidence from reliable sources (e.g., school data, student surveys, expert interviews) to support the initiative's necessity and feasibility. Proposals are reviewed quarterly by the Student Council and Principal.

materials.title: Student Survey Results: Reading Habits (Invented Teaching Example)
materials.text: A survey of 200 students (grades 6-8) conducted in October 2023 revealed: 65% of students wish they had more access to new books. 40% of students have books at home they no longer read. 75% of students would participate in a school book-swap program if available. (Source: School Library Committee, 2023)

materials.title: Article: Benefits of Book Swaps (Invented Teaching Example)
materials.text: A study published in 'Educational Review Journal' (Vol. 15, Issue 2, 2022) found that school book-swap programs significantly increase student engagement with reading by providing diverse, free access to literature. They also promote community and sustainability. (Source: Dr. A. Sharma, University of Education)

promptExamples.initial: Tell me about a book swap.
promptExamples.improved: Draft a proposal for a school book-swap program. Include evidence from at least two different sources to support why it's a good idea for students and the school. Explain how the program would work.
promptExamples.followup: Can you provide more specific data from the student survey to show the demand for new books?

activity.title: Improve Your Initiative Proposal
activity.instructions:
You have an initial draft for a school book-swap initiative. Your task is to improve it by adding strong evidence from the provided source cards and recording your changes.

1. Review the initial draft below.
2. Using at least two pieces of evidence from the source cards, revise the draft to make it more persuasive.
3. Keep a simple log of your improvements (e.g., 'Added survey data to show student interest').
activity.starter:
Initial Draft: Proposal for a School Book-Swap Program:
Our school needs a book-swap. Students like books. We can swap books. It will be good for everyone. It will help students get new books and share old ones.
activity.expectedEvidence: A revised proposal for a school book-swap program that clearly describes the initiative and uses at least two pieces of evidence from the provided source cards to support its claims. The student should also include a simple log detailing the improvements made to the initial draft.

quiz.question: Which type of information is generally considered the strongest evidence for a school initiative proposal?
options: A personal opinion from a friend.
A blog post from an unknown author.
quiz.explanation: Official school survey results are strong evidence because they are specific, verifiable, and directly reflect the opinions or needs of the school community. Personal opinions and unverified blog posts are less reliable.

quiz.question: According to the 'Student Survey Results: Reading Habits' source card, what percentage of students would participate in a school book-swap program?
quiz.explanation: The survey explicitly states that '75% of students would participate in a school book-swap program if available.' This is a direct fact from the source.

quiz.question: You want to propose a 'No-Waste Lunch Day' initiative. Which piece of evidence would best support the claim that food waste is a problem at your school?
options: A student's drawing of a full trash can.
Data from the cafeteria showing the amount of uneaten food thrown away daily.
A teacher saying 'kids waste too much food.'
quiz.explanation: Cafeteria data provides concrete, measurable evidence of food waste, making it the strongest support for your claim. A drawing is anecdotal, and a teacher's statement is an opinion, not specific data.

mission.title: Document Your 'Green Campus' Project
mission.instructions:
Imagine you want to start a 'Green Campus' project to reduce energy use at your school. Create a mini-proposal that includes:
1. The name and a brief description of your project.
2. At least one invented source-backed fact that supports your project (e.g., 'School electricity bills show a 15% increase in winter months').
3. A simple log of one improvement you made to your proposal (e.g., 'Added a specific statistic about energy waste').
4. A disclosure stating whether you used any AI tools to help write your proposal (e.g., 'I used AI to brainstorm ideas' or 'I did not use AI').
rubric: Project name and description are clear.
At least one invented, source-backed fact is included.
A simple improvement log is present.

hints.question: What kind of evidence should I look for?
hints.answer: Look for facts, data, or expert opinions that directly relate to your initiative. Official reports, surveys, or statistics are often very strong.

hints.question: How do I know if a source is reliable?
hints.answer: Check who created the information. Is it an organization, an expert, or a government body? Is the information recent? Does it seem balanced and fair?

hints.question: My proposal feels weak. What can I do?
hints.answer: Go back to your sources. Can you find more specific numbers, dates, or quotes that make your points undeniable? The more concrete your evidence, the stronger your proposal.

educatorNotes.sampleAnswer:
Activity Sample Answer:
Revised Proposal for a School Book-Swap Program:
Our school needs a book-swap program to increase reading access and promote sustainability. The program would allow students to exchange books they've finished for new ones, fostering a love for reading without cost.

Evidence:
1. According to the 'Student Survey Results: Reading Habits' (Source: School Library Committee, 2023), 65% of students wish they had more access to new books, and 75% would participate in a book-swap. This directly shows a high demand and willingness to engage.
2. An article in 'Educational Review Journal' (Source: Dr. A. Sharma, 2022) states that book-swap programs 'significantly increase student engagement with reading' and 'promote community and sustainability.' This expert opinion reinforces the educational and environmental benefits.
3. Furthermore, the 'School Policy on Student Initiatives' (Source: School Board, 2023) notes that student participation in extracurricular reading has declined by 10%, highlighting a school-wide need that this initiative can address.

Improvement Log:
- Added specific survey data (65% wish for books, 75% would participate) to show student interest and need.
- Included expert opinion from 'Educational Review Journal' to support the benefits of book swaps.
- Referenced school policy and internal report data (10% decline in reading programs) to align with school priorities and demonstrate necessity.

Mission Sample Answer:
Project Name: Green Campus Energy Savers
Description: This project aims to reduce our school's electricity consumption by encouraging simple habits like turning off lights and unplugging devices when not in use, and exploring options for energy-efficient lighting.

Invented Source-Backed Fact:
School electricity bills from the last year (Facilities Department, 2023) show that our school's energy consumption increased by 12% in the last year, costing an additional $1,500. This provides concrete proof that there's a problem we need to address and potential savings to be made.

Improvement Log:
- Added a specific statistic about the increase in electricity costs to make the financial impact clear.

AI Disclosure:
I did not use any AI tools to help write this proposal.
educatorNotes.commonMisconception: Students often confuse opinion or anecdotal evidence with factual, verifiable evidence. They might think 'everyone agrees' is enough, rather than needing specific data or expert statements.
reviewChecks: Does the proposal clearly state the initiative's purpose?
Are at least two distinct pieces of evidence included?
Is the evidence directly relevant to the initiative?
Does the student explain *how* the evidence supports their claims?
Are sources for the evidence clearly identified?
Is the language clear and persuasive?
educatorNotes.safetyNotes: Remind students that when conducting surveys or interviews for real projects, they must always follow school guidelines for privacy and consent, and never share personal information without permission. All sources should be treated with respect and cited properly.
